findings.reason: The protected app source introduces the exact generic local name index for a row and character position in source while constructing the next-occurrence table. The semantic compounds source_index and next_position are acceptable, but the standalone binding violates the campaign's explicit naming standard. The inert candidate renames only that binding and its uses to source_position; AST normalization proves there are no other changes, while both protected sources remain untouched.

With source_position, the candidate is clear, conventional, and interview-ready. The source_length, next_position, source_position, subsequences, source_index, character, letter, and position names expose preprocessing, current-copy progress, and restart state directly, and no generic local named index remains.

The table row next_position[i] records the earliest occurrence of every lowercase letter at or after source position i: copying row i + 1 preserves all later answers, and overwriting the current letter with i makes it earliest. For each target character, choosing the earliest occurrence available after source_index leaves at least as much suffix for later characters as any other valid choice, so one source copy consumes a maximum possible target prefix. If the current suffix has no occurrence, every construction must begin another source subsequence; restarting at row zero is therefore unavoidable. Absence even from row zero proves impossibility. Chosen positions increase within each copy, restarts concatenate valid subsequences, and every counted restart is necessary, so the returned count is minimum.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 1055, Python, and the native shortestWay(source, target) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms that a subsequence may delete any number of characters, including none, but must preserve relative order; the result is the minimum number of source subsequences whose concatenation equals target, or -1 when impossible. Both strings are nonempty, contain only lowercase English letters, and have lengths from 1 through 1000. The inert candidate preserves that exact contract.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2067432998 are algorithmically identical: both build the same 26-column suffix table from right to left, start one source copy at position zero, take the same earliest occurrence for each target character, restart only when the current suffix fails, reject a character absent from row zero, and return the same count. The candidate preserves that exact data flow and differs from the app source only by the semantic source_position rename; the native Solution.shortestWay wrapper is the only protected structural adaptation.

The three hidden workloads grow both source and target lengths from 32 to 512, a 16x span, with the only usable target letter at the end of source. This forces a repeated-full-source scan to traverse all S characters for every target character while the next-occurrence table performs O(AS+T) preprocessing and lookup with fixed A=26. In the final independent run, the exact candidate passed all 11 visible correctness cases and all three performance tiers with relative growth exponent -0.00 and a 0.99x largest ratio. An independently correct repeated-scan control matched every output but failed only performance with exponent +1.04 and a 50.65x largest ratio, cleanly distinguishing O(AS+T) from O(ST).

The Approach accurately defines the suffix next-occurrence table, derives earliest-position greediness, proves that each restart is unavoidable, handles missing characters, and defines S, T, and A. Its O(AS + T) time and O(AS) space claims match the candidate algorithm and branch manifest.

The modular Reference preserves the complete subsequence definition and positive/negative illustration, the minimum exact-concatenation objective, -1 impossibility behavior, all three source examples with every construction fact, both constraints, and the four-hint question-to-greedy-scan progression.

A fresh authenticated Premium review verified exactly three explained examples in source order, two constraints, four hints, and no notes, images, tables, diagrams, or follow-up. The modular files are hash-bound in source_fidelity.json to source content hash 6a6ef6b177738bc988ed37065cde31d2a9eb604fe832e49fd7fb31fbd94d6386, and the direct fidelity validator returns verified with no errors.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly three examples. All exact source, target, and output literals appear first in source order, including the two-copy construction, missing-character impossibility, and order-forced three-copy construction.

All 11 ordinary correctness cases are visible samples or trials. They cover the minimum length of 1 for both strings and the simultaneous maximum lengths of 1000, while the maximum-size correctness input remains a single easy subsequence rather than a performance workload.

Material behavior includes deleting no characters, deleting internal characters, one versus several source copies, a one-character source, repeated target characters, multiple useful occurrences within one source copy, reverse-order restarts, a missing character after a valid prefix, and exact concatenation of the complete target.

An independent repeated-pass oracle greedily consumes the longest possible target prefix from each fresh source copy and recomputed every authored expected result without using the protected suffix table.

The oracle, protected app source, inert naming-only candidate, and immutable native Solution agreed on all 14 authored correctness-plus-benchmark inputs, 15876 exhaustive nonempty binary source/target pairs through length six, 5000 deterministic random legal pairs, and six explicit minimum/maximum-length and impossibility boundary pairs. AST normalization independently proves that the candidate changes only index to source_position; the candidate also passed the complete real-test path.

The 32-, 128-, and 512-character workloads remain hidden and performance-only, use size consistently as both S and T, span 16x, and place one usable target letter at the end of source. A correct O(ST) repeated-scan control passed every output and failed only scaling against the O(AS+T) candidate.
